Critically, the lack of disorientation or amnesia *after calming* — combined with full responsiveness — strongly argues against true confusional arousals or sleep terrors, which classically feature *impaired responsiveness*, *prolonged confusion*, and *no memory of the event*. Instead, this pattern — abrupt fear-based awakening, preserved orientation *upon contact*, no autonomic storm, no motor complexity, and rapid return to calm — is atypical for classic NREM parasomnias. It is, however, highly characteristic of **nocturnal panic attacks**, especially in children who may lack insight into internal triggers and manifest fear somatically (e.g., as “something scary is happening” without identifiable dream content). While panic disorder is rare in young children, *nocturnal panic* can occur independently of daytime panic and is underrecognized in pediatrics. The absence of daytime anxiety symptoms does *not* rule it out — nocturnal panic often presents in isolation early on. Alternative explanations — nightmares (requires recall, orientation *immediately upon awakening*, not *after calming*), NFLE (requires EEG evidence; lacks stereotypy, eye signs, or post-ictal confusion), and behavioral insomnia alone (cannot explain the acute, fear-laden, mid-sleep awakenings) — are less consistent. - No description of child’s verbalization *during* episode (e.g., “I’m scared”, “I can’t breathe”, “Something’s wrong”) — would strongly support panic if present.
